newsitem.title: UK: RUGBY UNION-TWO SCOTTS HELP TO THWART SCOTLAND.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-TWO SCOTTS HELP TO THWART SCOTLAND.

text.p: Two Scotts took on Scotland at the weekend in a quartet of former rugby league exiles currently revitalising Welsh rugby union.

Scott Gibbs, Scott Quinnell, Allan Bateman and David Young were at the heart of Wales's first victory at Murrayfield since 1985, a decisive 34-19 win which has thrown the Five Nations' championship wide open.
And Jonathan Davies, the most famous defector of them all, also played a minor part, coming off the bench for the final four minutes in place of Gibbs.

''The rugby league boys bring a great mental attitude to the job,'' said Welsh captain Jonathan Humphreys. ''It's a long time since I have looked around the Welsh dressing room and seen everyone so confident.
''Some of Scott Gibbs's hits were phenomenal. There is a more mature outlook in the squad, as well as belief and determination.''
Davies's decision to throw in his lot with rugby league eight years ago was a body blow to a nation whose glory days of the 1970s were already a distant memory.
Disllusioned with the Welsh rugby establishment and anxious to ensure economic security for his family, Davies changed codes and carved out a successful career in the north of England.
A steady stream of irreplacable talent followed Davies across the border as the recession of the early 90s hit the Welsh valleys and Welsh rugby plunged to new depths.
Even Quinnell, son of former British Lion Derek, nephew of Barry John and godson of Mervyn Davies, succumbed, swapping derisory expenses at Llanelli for serious money at Wigan.
Professional rugby union, the consequence of an historic International Rugby Board meeting in Paris in August 1995 first stemmed then reversed the flow.
On Saturday Wales reaped the benefits, with centres Gibbs and Bateman in particular showing the mental and physical benefits of their rugby league experience.
Gibbs was immense in defence, tackling with the ferocity of a Western Samoan while Bateman made the initial break leading to Quinnell's opening try.

Quinnell himself was awesome with the ball in hand, repeatedly brushing aside some admittedly feeble Scotland tacklers, and he probably put paid to Scotland number eight Rob Wainwright's chances of captaining the British Lions in South Africa this year.
''Anything is possible now,'' said Quinnell. ''This team possesses terrific self-belief. We can return home with our heads held high and will relish tackling Ireland in two weeks' time.''
